title: An Exact Four-Wise Framework for Boomerang Cryptanalysis
authors: Chengcheng Chang, Kai Hu, Shuo Peng, and Haoyang Wang
abstract:
Boomerang cryptanalysis is inherently a four-point phenomenon, yet its recent geometric formulation relies on a 3-wise representation imposed by a quartet-sum-zero assumption. This simplification makes the transition matrices tractable, but it also removes boomerangs with unequal paired differences and prevents the framework from modeling impossible boomerang distinguishers.

We propose an exact 4-wise geometric framework for boomerang cryptanalysis that is a \emph{strict generalization} of the 3-wise framework: it recovers the 3-wise framework as the equal-difference $a=a',\,b=b'$ specialization, and at the same computational cost additionally covers the unequal-difference boomerangs and impossible boomerang distinguishers that the 3-wise representation cannot reach.
By choosing bases adapted to the two value coordinates and two difference coordinates of a boomerang quartet, our framework removes the 3-wise assumption and gives a unified transition-matrix description for both impossible boomerang distinguishers and fixed-key boomerang probabilities.

The framework has two concrete applications. First, it yields a positive (satisfiability) model for searching for impossible boomerang distinguishers from the difference coordinates in the 4-wise representation. Using this model, we find new impossible boomerang distinguishers for \present, \ascon, \skinny, and \gift.
Second, it computes fixed-key boomerang probabilities as sums of \emph{quasi-boomerang quartet characteristic} correlations. For the 13- and 17-round boomerang distinguishers of \skinny-64-128 and \skinny-64-192, respectively, the resulting probabilities match the experimental results and explain the gap left by the 3-wise framework through contributions from unequal-difference boomerangs.

1    Introduction
Differential cryptanalysis [11] is one of the most fundamental techniques in
modern symmetric-key cryptanalysis. It seeks high-probability differential char-
acteristics (DCs) whose probability is classically estimated as the product of
2       Chengcheng Chang, Kai Hu, Shuo Peng, and Haoyang Wang

one-round differential probabilities. Building on it, Wagner [42] introduced the
boomerang attack, which decomposes the target cipher as F = F1 ◦ F0 and
combines two short high-probability differentials of F0 and F1 into a longer dis-
tinguisher; it has since become a cornerstone of block cipher cryptanalysis [9,10].
    A complementary line of work studies the impossible variants of these at-
tacks, where the adversary exploits zero-probability events to discard wrong key
candidates. Lu [37,38] adapted the impossible-differential idea to the boomerang
setting and introduced the impossible boomerang attack (IBA). Its core ingre-
dient is an impossible boomerang distinguisher (IBD): a boomerang transition
(a, a′ ) → (b, b′ ) that no plaintext quartet can satisfy, obtained by a miss-in-the-
middle contradiction between two upper and two lower probability-one differen-
tials. After a decade of slow progress, the IBA has seen a sharp resurgence in the
last two years [46,14,30,15,18,31], and it is now an active branch of boomerang
cryptanalysis on equal footing with the classical (probability-p) boomerang.
    Despite their success, both branches rely on strong independence assump-
tions. The most notable ones are the Markov cipher assumption and the hypoth-
esis of stochastic equivalence [36]. These assumptions are convenient but are not
always justified. The true probability of a DC may deviate significantly from its
theoretical estimate, and in the boomerang setting, the gap can be even more
severe due to the additional coupling between the two halves. In the impossible
setting, an unjustified independence step is equally dangerous. It can declare
a quartet impossible when it is not, as recently witnessed by the disproof of a
SKINNY-128-384 IBD in [15]. Whether and when these assumptions hold has
therefore been the subject of intensive scrutiny.
    Among the various tools developed to address this question, the geometric
approach introduced by Beyne [4] has emerged as a particularly promising frame-
work. It interprets cryptanalytic techniques as linear operators acting on vector
spaces, with transition matrices arising from a change of basis. One concrete suc-
cess in this direction is the quasi-differential framework of Beyne and Rijmen [5],
which expresses the exact probability of a DC as the sum of correlations over
all quasi-differential trails (quasi-DCs), free of any Markov or independence as-
sumption. The framework has since been extended to integral cryptanalysis [6,7]
and higher-order differential-linear cryptanalysis [28], establishing the geometric
approach as a unifying language for symmetric-key cryptanalysis.
    The mix-basis variant of the geometric approach originates in Beyne’s the-
sis [4] and was taken up by Hu et al. [29] at CRYPTO 2025, who used different
bases for the input and output spaces. Soon after, Chang et al. [17] applied
this mix-basis framework to boomerang cryptanalysis, describing a boomerang
quartet as a 3-wise attack under the assumption that x1 ⊕ x2 ⊕ x3 ⊕ x4 = 0.
This assumption keeps the transition matrices tractable, but it collapses the
boomerang space into a 3-dimensional affine subspace. On the input side it
forces x1 ⊕ x2 = x3 ⊕ x4 , and on the output side it forces x1 ⊕ x4 = x2 ⊕ x3 .
As we now explain, this single restriction is the common bottleneck behind both
the fixed-key probability problem and the IBD search problem.
              An Exact Four-Wise Framework for Boomerang Cryptanalysis           3

Bottleneck 1. Fixed-key probability when the two differentials differ.
The 3-wise representation forces a = a′ on the input side and b = b′ on the
output side. It therefore covers only those boomerangs whose upper and lower
differentials share endpoints, and is structurally blind to the unequal-difference
case a ̸= a′ or b ̸= b′ , which is unavoidable in related-key cryptanalysis where
the key schedule may inject different differences into the two halves. For such
boomerangs the 3-wise framework returns no fixed-key probability at all. Wang
et al. [44] addressed this case by extending the quasi-differential framework to
quasi-d-differential cryptanalysis [41] and treating a boomerang as a quasi-3-
differential. The construction is exact but intractable: a boomerang viewed as a
3-differential leaves parts of its input and output free, generating an enormous
number of quasi-3-differential trails with tiny correlations, and [44] reports no
concrete distinguisher.
Bottleneck 2. Searching for impossible boomerang distinguishers. The
same a = a′ , b = b′ restriction makes the 3-wise representation blind to all IBDs
whose contradiction relies on unequal differences in the upper or lower half. The
same shortcoming surfaces, in a different language, in the use of the Double
Boomerang Connectivity Table (DBCT) [25,45]: Bonnetain and Lallemand [15]
showed that the DBCT only certifies impossibility under the equal-difference
constraint, and used this to disprove one of the SKINNY-128-384 IBDs claimed
by Zhang et al. [46].
    After Lu’s original manual constructions [37,38] and Choy and Yap’s exten-
sion [19] to generalized Feistel structures, the topic lay dormant for a decade.
The recent resurgence has produced several dedicated search tools, each cipher-
specific or limited in scope. Bonnetain et al. [14] gave ad-hoc contradiction
constructions for SIMON and SKINNYee. Hu et al. [30] developed a framework
that interleaves differential-, state-, and table-based propagations, reaching more
rounds at the price of an intricate construction with cipher-specific propagation
rules. In parallel, the wave of work on IB key recovery [18,31] has sharpened the
need for a clean and cipher-agnostic IBD-search tool, since the quality of the
underlying IBD bounds the reach of any subsequent key recovery.
    As a consequence, a simple and unified theoretical tool for boomerang crypt-
analysis is still missing, both for impossible boomerang distinguishers and for
boomerang cryptanalysis in the fixed-key model. The contrast with impossible
differential cryptanalysis, which has long enjoyed clean and cipher-agnostic auto-
mated search [26], makes this gap especially conspicuous. The 4-wise framework
developed below closes it, putting impossible boomerang search on the same
methodological footing as impossible differential search.


Our contributions. We propose an exact 4-wise geometric framework for
boomerang cryptanalysis that is a strict generalization of the 3-wise frame-
work of [17]: setting u2 = u3 and v2 = v3 together with the quartet-sum-
zero constraint recovers their construction, and at the same computational cost
our framework additionally covers the unequal-difference and impossibility cases
that the 3-wise representation cannot reach, resolving both bottlenecks above.

Application I. A positive SAT model for IBDs (Section 4). The frame-

an impossible pattern in Fm . The model finds new RK-IBDs covering 5 rounds

Application II. Exact fixed-key boomerang probability (Section 5).
Without any assumption, the framework returns the exact fixed-key proba-

of [17] is significantly off as it ignores the unequal-difference contributions.

intricate and the propagation rules are cipher-specific, making the framework

    The situation contrasts sharply with impossible differential cryptanalysis,
which has long enjoyed clean and cipher-agnostic automated search [26]. The
4-wise framework developed in this paper closes this gap, giving impossible
boomerang search the same level of clean and uniform methodology.


2.2   Geometric Approach

Beyne [4,3] proposed the geometric approach, a unified tool for various crypt-
analysis techniques. It has been applied to linear cryptanalysis [3], differential
cryptanalysis [5], and integral cryptanalysis [6,8]. In this framework, cryptan-
alytic methods are interpreted as linear operators acting on vector spaces of
functions, represented in different choices of basis. Cryptanalytic techniques dif-
fer in how many cipher values they jointly sample. Linear cryptanalysis acts on
one value, differential cryptanalysis on a pair, and boomerang cryptanalysis on a
quartet. Hu et al. [29] organize this by the dimension of the input sample space.

Quartet-level modeling in the 4-wise framework. To study this second
case, the difference-level positive model is no longer sufficient. Indeed, the im-
possibility is no longer explained by the absence of valid difference propagation,
but by the fact that no compatible quartet exists for the fixed input/output can-
didates. Therefore, we refine the search from difference pairs to quartet variables
and model the boomerang directly at the value level.
    In our 4-wise language, such a quartet can be represented by two differences
together with two values, namely (x1 , x3 , a, a′ ), which is essentially equivalent
to the state-based modeling used by Hu et al. [30]. Thus, rather than explicitly
enumerating quasi-BQCs and checking the cancellation of their correlations, we
formulate an UNSAT-based search model on quartets: if no quartet satisfies the
propagation constraints under the fixed input/output candidates for all keys,
then the corresponding boomerang distinguisher is impossible.
    This viewpoint is fully consistent with the exact 4-wise framework. It provides
a quartet-level realization of the same boomerang event and naturally comple-
ments the difference-level positive model developed in the previous subsections.
Results for GIFT-64 and SKINNY-64-192. We applied this quartet-level model
to the longer distinguishers reported by Hu et al. [30], in particular for GIFT-
64 and SKINNY-64-192. As in their work, the modeling exploits the linear key
schedule in the related-key setting. The key schedule is used to enforce several
rounds of all-zero propagation in the upper and lower parts, so that only a small
number of middle rounds contain non-zero differences. These middle rounds form
the core of the distinguisher, where the round-key differences introduce only one
active cell at the input and output of the core, respectively.
    Based on this structure, we build the quartet constraints for the core rounds
and connect them with the deterministic zero-difference propagation induced by
the linear key schedule. In this way, the search remains focused on the quartet-
level feasibility of the core, while still describing the full distinguisher within a
unified 4-wise formulation.
    We implemented the above quartet-level model and compared the results
with those of Hu et al. [30]. The comparison shows that our framework not only
recovers their distinguishers, but also finds additional ones in the same setting.
For SKINNY-64-192, Hu et al. reported 3 19-round IBDs, whereas our model
finds 5 in total. All of these 5 IBDs are given in Appendix A. For GIFT-64, we
find 48 13-round IBDs, as Hu et al.’s result. All of these 48 IBDs are given in
Appendix B. Therefore, even when restricted to the same quartet-level search
setting, the exact 4-wise framework leads to a larger set of valid IBDs for the
cipher instances.
    These results further illustrate the practical strength of the 4-wise framework.
On the one hand, the positive model of Section 4.2 efficiently captures direct
impossibility at the difference level. On the other hand, the quartet-level model
developed here handles longer distinguishers that rely on value-level infeasibility,
as in [30].

the fixed-key probability of a boomerang distinguisher is obtained by summing
